body:
Why a backup is necessary

A backup is a separate copy of important information that can be used to restore the information after accidental deletion, device failure, damage or a cyberattack. A backup is especially useful when ransomware prevents access to the original files.

Suppose a student's notes and certificates are stored only on one device. If ransomware locks that device's files, the student may be unable to access any of those documents. A previously created, usable backup provides another possible source for recovery.

Data backup is the practice of making and maintaining a separate recoverable copy of important information to reduce the risk of permanent data loss.

What makes a backup useful?

  • Regular creation: Back up files often enough that a recent copy is available when needed.
  • Separate storage: Keep a copy away from the original device, such as on securely managed cloud storage or an external storage device that is disconnected when not in use.
  • Protection: Restrict unauthorised access to the backup. A backup containing personal information requires appropriate security.
  • Recovery testing: Check occasionally that important files can actually be restored from the backup.

A copy permanently connected to the infected device may also be affected by some attacks. Therefore, keeping a separately protected copy is more useful than merely creating another folder on the same device.

Software updates and genuine applications

Software may contain weaknesses that can be exploited by attackers. A security update may correct such weaknesses and reduce the risk of compromise. Users should keep the operating system, browser and frequently used applications updated through genuine sources.

Downloading an application from an unsolicited link is risky because the application may be fraudulent or malicious. Users should verify the publisher and avoid granting unnecessary access to contacts, messages, files or other personal information.

Security applications can help identify malicious content, but they do not replace careful behaviour. A device may remain at risk if its owner voluntarily gives a criminal a password or payment authorisation.

Remote-access fraud

Some fraudsters pretend to offer technical assistance, refunds or banking help and persuade the victim to install a remote-access or screen-sharing application. Such software can have legitimate uses, but granting control to an untrusted person may allow that person to view sensitive activity or misuse the device.

The important distinction is between the tool and its use. A legitimate remote-support application is not necessarily malware. Nevertheless, allowing a stranger to operate a device during banking or payment activity creates a serious risk.

Safe action after suspected compromise

If malicious software is suspected, the user should stop sensitive activity on the affected device and seek trustworthy help to remove the threat. Important account passwords should be changed using a device believed to be safe. If a bank account or payment credential may be affected, the bank should be contacted promptly through an official channel.

Files should be restored from a backup only after the malicious software has been addressed. Otherwise, the restored information may become inaccessible again. Relevant messages, transaction details and other evidence should be preserved if fraud has occurred.

Different protective measures solve different problems. Strong authentication reduces unauthorised account access. Updates and security tools reduce certain software risks. Backups help restore information after data loss. No single measure replaces all the others.

Prelims focus

  • A backup is a separate recoverable copy of data.
  • Backups primarily help with recovery and availability.
  • A separate protected backup is preferable to relying only on the original device.
  • Security updates can correct weaknesses in software.
  • Remote-access applications can be misused to observe or control a victim's device.
  • Trap: A backup does not prevent password theft, and antivirus software cannot prevent every form of social engineering.

[CERT-In, Cyber Swachhta Kendra, Botnet Cleaning and Malware Analysis Centre, guidance on genuine software, safe links and regular backups against ransomware; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2022-0014, Mobile Based Malware: Methods and Countermeasures, 30 May 2022; Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, 28 January 2022, sections on remote-access applications and safe digital banking practices. Consulted 17 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A separate usable backup can provide a recovery path when the original files become unavailable.

title: Backups, Security Updates and Safe Device Practices

body:
UPI and digital payments

UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface. It is an instant payment system developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) that enables transfers between bank accounts through participating applications and banks.

UPI allows individuals and businesses to make and receive payments conveniently. However, criminals may exploit a user's misunderstanding of how payments are authorised.

UPI ID, UPI PIN and OTP: different purposes

TermPurposeSecurity rule
UPI IDIdentifies a payment address associated with a UPI account.May be shared when necessary to receive a payment; it is not the secret used to authorise a debit.
UPI PINA secret personal identification number used to authorise UPI payments or other permitted debit operations.Must not be disclosed to another person.
OTPA temporary verification code used for an authorised authentication or transaction-related process.Must not be shared with callers, strangers or fraudulent websites.

Knowing someone's UPI ID is not the same as knowing that person's UPI PIN. A UPI ID identifies where a payment can be directed; the PIN helps authorise a debit from an account.

Receiving money is different from paying money

The most important practical distinction is that receiving an ordinary UPI transfer does not require the recipient to enter a UPI PIN. Entering a UPI PIN generally authorises money to leave the payer's account.

SituationWhat happens?UPI PIN required from the person receiving money?
Receiving a normal transferAnother person sends money to the recipient's UPI address or displayed QR code.No.
Making a paymentThe payer selects a recipient, checks the amount and authorises a debit.Not applicable; the payer normally authorises using the PIN, while modes such as UPI LITE allow payments without a UPI PIN.
Approving a collect requestThe person receiving the request approves a debit from their own account.No money is being received by that person; approval authorises payment.

A collect request is a request to the payer to approve sending money. A legitimate collect request may be used for payment. Person-to-person (P2P) UPI collect requests were discontinued from 1 October 2025. The fraud occurs when the criminal falsely describes that approval as a necessary step for receiving money.

Common forms of UPI and OTP fraud

Fake cashback or refund

A criminal promises a reward or refund and asks the victim to scan a QR code and enter a UPI PIN. This instruction is suspicious because scanning another person's payment QR code and authorising with a PIN is used for making a payment, not receiving a reward.

Fraudulent collect request

In this historical fraud pattern, a buyer claims to be transferring money to a seller but instead sends a collect request. If the seller approves the request and enters the PIN, the seller may authorise money to leave their own account.

Fake customer support and remote access

A fraudster may appear as a bank or payment-service representative and claim that a failed payment, refund or KYC issue requires an OTP, UPI PIN or remote-access application. These demands can be used to steal credentials or gain control of payment activity. Customer-service contact details should be obtained independently from genuine sources.

False payment confirmation

A seller should not rely only on a screenshot or payment-success image shown by a buyer. Such an image may be altered or unrelated to the claimed transfer. Receipt should be checked through the seller's own trusted UPI application, banking transaction history or genuine bank notification.

Practical safeguards before authorising a payment

  1. Open a trusted UPI application and check the name or payment address of the intended recipient.
  2. Read the transaction amount and determine whether the action is a payment or an incoming request for payment.
  3. Enter the UPI PIN only to authorise a transaction that the user has deliberately chosen.
  4. Do not disclose the PIN or OTP to any person, including someone claiming to be a bank employee.
  5. Check the actual transaction record rather than depending on another person's claim that payment has succeeded.

QR-code distinction: A merchant may display their own QR code so a customer can pay them. The merchant does not need to scan a QR code supplied by the customer or enter a UPI PIN merely to receive that payment.

Prelims focus

  • UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface.
  • UPI was developed by the National Payments Corporation of India.
  • A UPI ID identifies a payment address; a UPI PIN authorises a debit.
  • A normal incoming UPI transfer does not require the recipient's UPI PIN.
  • Approving a collect request can authorise money to leave the approver's account.
  • Trap: Scanning a stranger's QR code and entering a UPI PIN is not a required method of receiving cashback or a refund.

[National Payments Corporation of India, UPI: Frequently Asked Questions, sections What is UPI? and What is a UPI-PIN?; National Payments Corporation of India, Fraud Awareness, sections on fake cashback links and QR codes; Reserve Bank of India, Consumer Awareness: Cyber Threats and Frauds, 28 January 2022, sections on misuse of UPI collect requests, unauthorised QR codes and remote-access fraud. Consulted 17 November 2026.]
